# Embedded Systems and IoT Laboratories

Four Arduino exercises rebuilt as one testable C++17 project. The logic — button edges,
stopwatch transitions, ADC filtering, UART command parsing — lives in a
hardware-independent core; the sketches contain pin numbers and I/O and nothing else.

**20 tests pass on a laptop before a wire is connected.**

## The move that makes it possible

Embedded coursework is usually untestable for one structural reason: the logic is written
inside `loop()`, where it can only be reached by a board. Lifting it out is the whole
design — [[separating-computation-from-io]] and
[[pure-domain-engine-shared-across-hosts]] applied to a microcontroller, with the sketch
as one host and the native test binary as the other.

The core has no Arduino dependency, no heap allocation, no exceptions and no blocking
calls. That list is not minimalism for its own sake; each entry is a constraint that an
8-bit target imposes and that a desktop compiler will happily let you violate.

## The four labs and the failure each one prevents

| Lab | State machine | Failure prevented |
|---|---|---|
| 01 · Button counter | independent debouncers + bounded counter | bounce-driven double counts, and `while`-loop lockups waiting for release |
| 02 · Stopwatch | reset → running → paused | elapsed time lost across pause/resume |
| 03 · Voltage monitor | moving average + sample scheduler | single-sample noise, and the 1024-vs-1023 conversion error |
| 04 · UART LED | strict parser + non-blocking blinker | prefix commands accepted, invalid intervals, blocking `delay()` |

The 1024-vs-1023 one is the classic. A 10-bit ADC returns 0–1023, so full scale is code
`1023`, not `1024`; dividing by the wrong constant produces a reading that is plausible,
consistently slightly wrong, and never noticed on a lab bench.

## Three rules that generalise

**Events, not sleeps.** Debouncing and blinking are timestamp-driven. `delay()` is not a
timing primitive, it is a promise that nothing else happens — which on a single-threaded
controller means serial input dropped and a display not refreshed while an LED is
"blinking".

**One clock rule: always `now - then`.** Every scheduler compares elapsed time using
unsigned subtraction. The natural-looking `now > then + interval` overflows and fails
around the 49.7-day `millis()` rollover, and unsigned wraparound makes the subtraction form
correct *through* the rollover rather than in spite of it. This is a bug with a 49.7-day
reproduction time, which is to say a bug that is never reproduced.

**Reject, do not guess.** The UART parser accepts exactly `LED ON`, `LED OFF`,
`LED STATUS` and `LED BLINK <20..60000>`. Extra suffixes, partial numbers, empty intervals
and overlong lines are refused. A parser that accepts a prefix is a parser that will one
day act on a truncated transmission.

## Verification

`scripts/test.ps1` or `scripts/test.sh`, needing only a C++17 `g++`; build products go to
the OS temporary directory rather than the repository. Expected output is literally
`20 tests passed`.

`tools/` generates a deterministic state trace for all four labs — the headless
counterpart to the SVG guide in `assets/`, and the thing to read when no board or LCD is
available. Compare [[make-the-formal-object-observable]]: a state machine you can print is
a state machine you can argue about.

A 2026-08-12 local audit passed the warning-as-error C++17 build and all 20 native tests. The
headless trace then exercised the documented button, stopwatch, voltage-monitor, and UART states.
The run used an external temporary root because the sandbox cannot use the owner's Temp directory;
that is a test-host restriction, not evidence of board validation.
